children: By Alexander Osipovich, Rory Jones and Patricia Kowsmann

The U.S. has tried for years to cut off its adversaries from the world's financial system. But money from places such as Iran and Russia has kept on flowing — in large part thanks to banks in China, people familiar with the activity say.

The challenge is exemplified by a little-known regional bank in eastern China, which in recent years emerged as a key conduit for Iranian and Russian financial transactions, according to former U.S. officials and documents seen by The Wall Street Journal. The funds were used to buy Chinese goods in violation of Western sanctions, including some with potential military applications, the documents show.

The bank, Zhejiang Chouzhou Commercial Bank, was flagged internally by U.S. officials during both the Biden and Trump administrations for facilitating transactions that appeared designed to evade sanctions, former officials said. ZCCB stood out from other Chinese banks for how frequently it came up in U.S. monitoring of Iranian and Russian money flows, they said.

But Washington stopped short of slapping ZCCB with sanctions. It was difficult to determine whether ZCCB knew about the funds' origins, and Washington worried that targeting the bank could upset relations with Beijing or disrupt China's financial system, the former officials said.

The U.S. faces similar dilemmas in dealing with several other Chinese banks involved in trade with Russia and Iran, current and former officials say. The Treasury Department in October 2025 said Chinese bank accounts were the main source of roughly $5 billion that Iranian shell companies moved around the world in the prior year.
ZCCB said in response to questions from the Journal that it has always adhered to Chinese law and closely monitored international regulation.

"We are committed to conducting business in compliance with applicable laws and regulations, including applicable anti-money-laundering, counterterrorist financing, and sanctions risk management requirements," ZCCB said.
China says it abides by international law in trade with Iran and Russia, but it rejects what it describes as unilateral American sanctions against the countries.

Documents seen by the Journal show Iranian companies attempting to send money to ZCCB, routing it through what the U.S. government calls a Tehran-backed shadow banking network. Other documents show that ZCCB was a frequent destination for payments made through A7, a Russian sanctions-evasion network that was labeled a "significant transnational criminal organization" by the Treasury last month.
The documents don't show whether ZCCB's management knew the funds involved sanctioned entities in Iran and Russia, whose roles were obscured behind a web of front companies and intermediaries.

Experts say the flows expose a weak point in U.S. sanctions, highlighting how China bolsters America's main geopolitical rivals. Beijing has been a key trading partner for both Iran and Russia, buying their oil, selling them electronics and other goods, and giving them a foothold in the global financial system through Chinese banks.

"There is no policy appetite to sanction these banks, which would be perceived as an escalation by China," said Alex Zerden, a former Treasury official during Trump's first term and founder of advisory firm Capitol Peak Strategies.

"At present, the actions do not match the rhetoric of Economic D-Day, Economic Outcast or Economic Fury," he said, referring to the Trump administration's efforts to isolate Iran through ever-tighter sanctions.
Any foreign bank that facilitates Iran's access to global money flows risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system, a Trump administration official said.
"No institution is beyond the reach of U.S. sanctions," the official said.
Making deals
U.S. sanctions limit what Iranian and Russian entities can buy and sell abroad, so they have largely stopped trading with the West, instead buying goods from Chinese suppliers.
To pay for them, they have to find a bank willing to accept the funds, which could expose that institution to U.S. penalties. That is where banks such as ZCCB come in.

In February 2025, a now-defunct company in the former Soviet republic of Kyrgyzstan agreed to pay around $1.5 million to a Chinese supplier for 40,000 kilograms of molybdenum trioxide, according to an invoice seen by the Journal.

A metallic compound, molybdenum trioxide can be used to make tough, heat-resistant alloys used in armored vehicles or missile engines. The shipment was to be delivered by truck from China to St. Petersburg in Russia, the invoice shows.

The buyer, called Trading Company of the Kyrgyz Republic, paid for the shipment in two installments to be deposited at the supplier's account at ZCCB, according to payment records seen by the Journal. Trading Company of the Kyrgyz Republic has been described by U.S. officials as one of hundreds of front companies for A7, the Russian sanctions-evasion network.

The invoice and payment records were part of a trove of internal A7 files made public after hackers attacked the Russian network and released chat messages among its employees. Those chats led researchers to an unsecured drive where an A7 developer had left thousands of files exposed to the public internet.

Out of some 3,500 transactions detailed in those A7 documents, ZCCB was the most frequently occurring bank for the receipt of payments, said Zachary Tvarozna, an independent researcher who analyzed the files.
"It's a village bank that came out of nowhere and is now on the receiving end of a lot of A7's activities," Tvarozna said.

The transactions detailed in the A7 documents took place from late 2024 to mid-2025, and included purchases of civilian goods such as cars and clothing as well as items with potential military uses, such as electronics used in drone warfare.

ZCCB told the Journal that it had launched a new round of internal investigations in light of the Treasury's latest sanctions against A7 in early October, and that it couldn't confirm that relevant funds originated in Russia.

A7 didn't respond to a request for comment. In a statement posted to social media in early October, A7 said it was created "to ensure uninterrupted payments for the Russian market, which has been subjected to illegal restrictions."
A separate set of documents reviewed by the Journal show how Iranian companies sought to use ZCCB.

In December 2023, an Iranian manufacturer called Saab Steel Development agreed to pay $101,297.46 for coiled sheets of steel from a Shanghai-based supplier, according to an invoice seen by the Journal.

The supplier's bank was ZCCB, and the steel was to be delivered to Iran's port of Bandar Abbas over the next year, the invoice shows. The U.S. has repeatedly issued sanctions targeting Iranian industry and steel imports.

Two payment orders from April 2024 show the next steps. The manufacturer first instructed Bank Tejarat, an Iranian state-owned bank, to send $101,297.46 to the supplier's ZCCB account. Bank Tejarat then requested the payment be made through a money changer called Sadaf Exchange, which U.S. officials say operates numerous shell companies to make and receive payments on Iran's behalf.
Based on the documents viewed by the Journal, it couldn't be determined which company was supposed to send the payment, or if ZCCB ultimately received it.
ZCCB said it has never received any funds remitted from Sadaf Exchange but declined to answer further questions about transactions detailed by the Journal.

The U.S. sanctioned Bank Tejarat in January 2012 and Sadaf Exchange in June 2024. Tejarat, Sadaf and Saab didn't respond to requests for comment. Tejarat has said it complies with international law and works in the interest of the Iranian economy.

The elaborate system makes it difficult for banks to know payments are connected to Iran, said Miad Maleki, a former senior Treasury official now at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank.
"By the time the money arrives, it has usually passed through several layers," he said.
Rapid growth

Founded in 1987, ZCCB has grown rapidly along with the boom in exports from its original base in Yiwu, a city in eastern China that is home to the world's largest marketplace for wholesale goods. From 2018 to 2024, income from international payment transactions grew from 2% to nearly 12% of total revenue, the bank's filings show. China has a history of letting smaller banks deal with risky countries such as Iran and Russia, former U.S. officials said. That way, if the U.S. decides to sanction a Chinese institution, its actions would only affect less-important players, while letting China's biggest banks stay in Washington's good graces.

In 2012, the Obama administration cut off one Chinese lender, Bank of Kunlun, from transacting in dollars — the ultimate weapon the U.S. can wield against a foreign bank — for its dealings with Iran. Beijing said it was "strongly dissatisfied" with the move and Kunlun said the U.S. sanctions violated international norms.
The U.S. has avoided sanctioning other Chinese banks for Iran ties, despite concerns that several were involved in transactions with the country, former U.S. officials said.

ZCCB drew attention from Treasury soon after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, when evidence emerged that it was facilitating trade with Russia's defense industry, former officials said. An executive order signed by Joe Biden in December 2023 threatened to sanction foreign banks involved in financing Russia's military-industrial base.
ZCCB said it cut ties with Russian clients shortly afterward.

The A7 documents show ZCCB's links to Russia resumed in 2024, although indirectly, through front companies and banks in countries such as Kyrgyzstan. ZCCB said last year it stopped setting up new correspondent banking relationships in Kyrgyzstan.

An analysis by U.S.-based financial intelligence firm TRM Labs showed a similar picture for Iran. TRM examined thousands of documents published by WikiIran, a website that posts leaked payment instructions, invoices and transaction records from companies allegedly involved in Iranian trade. The leaks don't purport to cover all of Iran's money flows.

TRM identified more than 900 accounts at Chinese banks named in the documents as destinations for Iran-linked payments between 2021 and mid-2025. Some 240 of the accounts were held at ZCCB, while another roughly 670 involved other Chinese banks, according to TRM.
ZCCB disputed the accuracy of WikiIran, saying it had reviewed the website and found references to some accounts that didn't belong to it.
